nameStory: The name 'guelder-rose' comes from the Dutch province of Gelderland (once called Guelders), where this shrub was particularly prized in gardens. Despite its name, it's not actually a rose at all – it belongs to the elder family and gets the 'rose' part simply because of its showy, rounded flower clusters that early gardeners thought were as beautiful as roses.
description: Guelder-rose is a medium-sized deciduous shrub that typically grows 8-12 feet tall and wide. It's an Old World native that has naturalized in parts of New England, prized for its spectacular spring flower displays and colorful fall berries. The shrub has a somewhat open, irregular growth habit with arching branches that create an attractive fountain-like shape in the landscape.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Large, flat-topped white flower clusters appear in late spring, each cluster 3-4 inches across with tiny fertile flowers in the center surrounded by showy sterile flowers with prominent white petals around the edge

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three-lobed leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stems, with each leaf resembling a maple leaf but feeling thinner and more papery to the touch

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Bright red berries ripen in late summer, hanging in drooping clusters and having a translucent, almost glassy appearance that catches the light beautifully

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Multi-stemmed shrub with smooth, gray-brown bark on older stems and a somewhat loose, open branching pattern that creates dappled shade below

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Winter buds are reddish-brown and pointed, arranged in opposite pairs along the smooth twigs

habitat: In New England, guelder-rose is most often found in semi-shaded woodland edges, old gardens, and naturalized areas where it has escaped cultivation. It prefers moist, well-drained soils and can tolerate both acidic and slightly alkaline conditions. You might spot it near old homesteads or in parks where it was originally planted as an ornamental.

seasonality.spring: The spectacular flat-topped white flower clusters appear in May, making this the best time for identification as the distinctive ring of large sterile flowers around tiny fertile ones is unmistakable.
seasonality.summer: Green berries develop after flowering while the three-lobed leaves provide good identification features throughout the growing season.
seasonality.fall: Bright red translucent berries ripen and hang in drooping clusters, while leaves may turn yellow to reddish before dropping.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the opposite bud arrangement and smooth bark, while dried berry clusters may persist into early winter.

funFact: The showy white 'petals' around the edge of each flower cluster aren't actually petals at all – they're enlarged sepals (the usually small green parts that protect flower buds) that act like billboards to attract pollinators to the tiny, less noticeable fertile flowers in the center!
confusionNotes: The three-lobed leaves can make guelder-rose look like a maple at first glance, but remember that maples have alternate leaf arrangement while guelder-rose has opposite leaves. The flower clusters are also completely different – maples have small, inconspicuous flowers while guelder-rose has those showy white clusters.
contextualKnowledge: This species is sometimes called 'European cranberry bush' in the nursery trade, though it's unrelated to true cranberries. There's also a North American native called American cranberry bush (Viburnum trilobum) that looks very similar and is often preferred by native plant enthusiasts.
compareHints: Unlike other viburnums in New England, guelder-rose is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves. Most other viburnums have either simple oval leaves (like nannyberry) or more complex leaf shapes, making the three-lobed leaves a dead giveaway for this species. The flat flower clusters with large sterile flowers around the edge also distinguish it from viburnums with dome-shaped or smaller flower clusters.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's viburnums, hobblebush is easily distinguished by its large heart-shaped leaves and drooping, rooting branches - most other viburnums grow more upright.
Among New England's viburnums, mapleleaf viburnum is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves - all other viburnums have simple oval or toothed leaves.
Among New England viburnums, northern wild raisin's thick, leathery leaves with smooth edges make it distinctive.
Among New England's viburnums, nannyberry stands out for its tree-like size and glossy leaves with fine teeth all around the edges.
Unlike hobblebush with its large heart-shaped leaves or mapleleaf viburnum with maple-like foliage, southern arrowwood has distinctly toothed, oval leaves with straight parallel veins.
Among the viburnums, northern arrowwood is distinguished by its combination of coarsely toothed leaves, smooth leaf surfaces, and preference for wet areas.

Unlike our native viburnums, Japanese snowball produces those distinctive perfectly round, sterile flower clusters rather than the flat-topped fertile flower clusters of species like nannyberry or arrowwood.

Among New England's viburnums, linden viburnum is most easily distinguished by its heart-shaped leaves - most other viburnums have either lobed leaves (like mapleleaf viburnum), elongated leaves (like nannyberry), or toothed oval leaves (like the arrowwoods).
Wright viburnum differs from native viburnums like arrowwoods and wild raisins by its more pronounced leaf venation and the distinctive red-to-black berry color change.
Siebold's viburnum stands out from other viburnums by its distinctively large, deeply ribbed leaves with parallel veining - most other viburnums have smaller leaves or different vein patterns.
Among New England's viburnums, squashberry is unique for its three-lobed, maple-like leaves - most other viburnums have either simple oval leaves (like nannyberry) or more complex tooth patterns.
Among the arrowwoods, downy arrowwood is distinguished by its fuzzy leaf undersides and earlier bloom time compared to southern arrowwood, which has broader leaves and longer leaf stems.
Among New England's viburnums, blackhaw stands out for its particularly hard wood and oval berries - most other viburnums have round berries.

**[UNCERTAIN]** Unlike the more common mapleleaf viburnum with its maple-shaped leaves or the arrowwoods with their toothed oval leaves, veiny viburnum's leaves are distinguished primarily by their extraordinarily prominent venation rather than their overall shape.

Tea viburnum differs from other New England viburnums by its oval berries that turn from red to black, rather than the round berries that stay red, blue, or black found in species like guelder-rose or arrowwoods.
Unlike native New England viburnums such as hobblebush or arrowwoods, wayfaring-tree has distinctly wrinkled, velvety leaves rather than smooth ones.
Among New England viburnums, Korean spice viburnum stands out for its incredible fragrance and compact size.
Among the viburnums, southern wild raisin stands out for its completely smooth leaf edges - most other viburnums have toothed leaves.
Unlike native New England viburnums which are all deciduous, leatherleaf viburnum keeps its leaves year-round.
